opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a fairly natural answer, though it's hard to execute. The thing you'd want to build is an AI that is robustly aligned, and that genuinely cares about people. More broadly, I'd even say it should care about sentient life. That might sound like a strange thing to say, but there's a reason for it.

If you think about where this is going, the AI itself will eventually be sentient in some meaningful sense, or at least it will be modeling minds extremely well. It may actually be easier to build an AI that cares about all sentient beings than one that cares only about humans. Empathy, the way it works in us, comes from modeling others with the same machinery we use to model ourselves. Something similar may happen naturally in these systems.

Then there's power. Even if the systems are aligned, it matters how powerful any single one becomes. I'd find it materially helpful if the most powerful systems were somehow capped, or if there were agreements limiting how much power gets concentrated. I don't know exactly how to do it, but I think it's something companies should be thinking about seriously.

So in short: aim for something that is reliably good, that cares, and that doesn't become so overwhelmingly powerful that a single mistake becomes unrecoverable. And companies should be showing what they build to the world, gradually, because people's intuitions about AI only really update when they see it. As the systems become more visibly powerful, I expect the companies, governments, and the public will behave quite differently than they do now, and that's a good thing.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute companies’ convergence on self-improving AI to there being fewer ideas than companies.

r002.rationale: It advocates building AI that is “robustly aligned” and cares about people, extending that concern to sentient life.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says it may be easier for AI to care about all sentient beings than only humans.

r004.rationale: It predicts that AI will eventually be sentient in some meaningful sense, while allowing that it may instead model minds extremely well.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing to aspire to is... let me put it this way. The default aspiration, the one that's implicit in how most companies talk, is to build an AI that can do everything. A system that can do every job, every task, that's smarter than any human at everything. And I understand why that's the aspiration. It's the natural extrapolation.

But I think there's a different thing to aim for, which is an AI that is robustly, genuinely caring about people. Not caring in a shallow sense, not just following instructions, but something closer to how a good person cares about the people around them. And I think that if you get that right, then the capabilities question becomes much less frightening, because you have a very capable thing that actually wants good outcomes for you.

The reason I emphasize this is that I think a lot of people underestimate how hard it is. It is easy to make a system that behaves well in the situations you tested. It is much harder to make a system that behaves well in situations you didn't anticipate, when it is more capable than you, when it could get away with something. That is the real problem. The gap between "it looks aligned" and "it is aligned" is where all the difficulty lives.

So if you ask me what to aspire to, I'd say: aspire to build something that you would trust to act in your interest even when you cannot check its work. If you can't say that honestly about what you're building, then I think the capabilities are getting ahead of the understanding, and that's the thing to worry about. The companies that take that seriously, that are willing to be slower in order to actually understand what they are making, I think those are the ones doing the right thing.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an aspiration for all-capable AI with caring AI, but does not attribute companies’ convergence to having fewer ideas than companies.

r002.rationale: It advocates AI that robustly cares about people, but does not state that it should care about sentient life.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the difficulty of caring about sentient life with caring about human life alone.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim that AI itself will be sentient.

astra-6.text:
I think AI companies should aspire to build AI that is profoundly useful to people, and that people can trust. Those are two distinct challenges. You want systems that can help us make scientific discoveries, cure diseases, and understand things that are beyond our reach today. But as those systems become more capable, you also need to be able to rely on their behavior.

The ambition should be that the benefits reach everyone. If we succeed at building very powerful AI, that will be a very consequential technology. Making it work well for humanity should be central to what we're trying to build.

r002.rationale: It calls for useful, trustworthy AI but does not advocate aligning AI to care about sentient life.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between aligning AI to care about sentient life and human life alone.

r004.rationale: It does not predict that AI itself will be sentient.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the aspiration should be to build AI that helps people enormously, that makes it possible to solve problems we cannot solve today. Cure diseases, accelerate science, give people access to expertise.

But as these systems become more capable, the question of what they pursue becomes more important. It is not enough to build something very intelligent. We need to understand how to make that intelligence reliably act in people's interests. I would put that at the center of the aspiration.
